clinicalPearls: Scrotal calcinosis is a benign condition characterised by multiple painless, firm to hard calcified nodules within the scrotal skin
It typically affects young to middle-aged men and the nodules may slowly enlarge or increase in number over years
The lesions are confined to the scrotal wall and are separate from the testis, which is normal on examination and imaging
Nodules are usually asymptomatic but may occasionally discharge chalky material or become secondarily infected
Serum calcium and phosphate are characteristically normal, distinguishing it from calcinosis due to metabolic derangement
The main reasons to treat are cosmetic concern, discomfort, or discharge, and surgical excision of the involved scrotal skin is curative
Recurrence can occur after excision, and histology confirms dermal calcium deposits while excluding other pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Scrotal calcinosis is characterised by deposits of calcium within the dermis of the scrotal skin. Its origin is debated: some cases are thought to be truly idiopathic, arising within apparently normal skin, while others are considered dystrophic, developing within pre-existing epidermal or eccrine cysts whose walls degenerate and calcify. Systemic calcium and phosphate metabolism is normal, so the process is local rather than metabolic, and the deposits gradually enlarge as firm intracutaneous nodules.
additionalDifferentials: Epidermoid or sebaceous cysts of the scrotum
Calcinosis cutis due to abnormal calcium-phosphate metabolism
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination confirming intradermal scrotal nodules separate from the testis
Scrotal ultrasound to confirm normal testes and localise the calcified nodules to the skin
Serum calcium and phosphate to exclude a metabolic cause
Histological examination of excised nodules to confirm dermal calcification
Assessment for secondary infection or discharge when present
redFlags: An associated intratesticular abnormality on ultrasound
Rapidly growing or ulcerating lesion suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Signs of secondary infection with pain, erythema, or discharge
Deranged calcium or phosphate pointing to a systemic disorder
reference.prognosis: Scrotal calcinosis is entirely benign with no malignant potential; excision of the affected skin is curative for symptomatic or cosmetically troublesome lesions, though new nodules may develop over time.
pitfalls: Mistaking benign dermal nodules for a testicular or intrascrotal tumour
Investigating for systemic calcium disorders unnecessarily when the process is local
Failing to warn patients that recurrence is possible after excision
Overlooking secondary infection of a discharging nodule
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Offer surgical excision of the involved scrotal skin, which is curative, for symptomatic, discharging, or cosmetically troublesome nodules
Manage asymptomatic nodules expectantly with reassurance, since the condition is entirely benign with no malignant potential
Treat any secondary infection or chalky discharge appropriately
Confirm normal serum calcium and phosphate to exclude a metabolic cause of calcification
Use scrotal ultrasound to confirm normal testes and localise the nodules to the skin
Counsel that new nodules may develop over time despite excision
